WIBTA if I told my daughter to find a different hobby? | My daughter Ann (17) has been obsessed with building miniatures ever since she saw Hereditary a few months back. Since then, she has probably spent close to 500 dollars on miniature sets from Amazon, Hobby Lobby, and etsy. All of this money comes from her job at a local movie theatre, so I can't exactly cut her off. I can't explain why, but something about it drives me up the \*\*\*\*ing wall. Maybe it's because Toni Collette was so creepy? Maybe I just want to spend some quality time with my daughter instead of watching her waste her life in her bedroom. I hear my sister talk about dropping her daughter off at soccer, or how her son's the lead in the school play, and then think about how my daughter's upstairs building a tiny cottage with tweezers. She hasn't ever really shown interest in any hobbies before, so I thought it would be grateful that she's finally good at something, but mostly I'm just annoyed. Her grades are fine (Bs), her chores are always done, but mostly every second of her spare time is spent putting together miniatures. I try to ask her if she'd like to go for a walk with me, or sign up for cheerleading, but she always says no. My husband thinks its sweet and has started letting her put them around the house and in his office at work. Every day, I drink coffee next to a 60 dollar miniature greenhouse, and think about when the last time I had a genuine conversation with my daughter that didn't revolve around the merits of craft glue versus hot glue was. ​ I know I'm probably the asshole, but would I be the asshole if I asked her to find another hobby that might help her in life? Like something she could stick on a resume?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 ( the asshole)** *(Here's why, with clarity and compassion)* ### **Why it's " the asshole" behavior:** - **You're pathologizing a harmless, skill-based hobby.** Miniatures aren't "waste of life"—they involve **precision, creativity, patience, and problem-solving**. Many careers (architecture, set design, art restoration, even engineering) stem from such hobbies. Telling her it's "waste" dismisses her agency and intelligence. - **You're using "future prospects" as a controlling excuse.** Hobbies don't need to "help her in life" to be valid. * "What if she's building a miniature greenhouse because she's an aspiring architect? Or just enjoys the meditative process?"* Forcing her to "find a resume-friendly hobby" reduces her to a tool for your anxieties, not a person. - **You're not addressing the real issue: disconnection.** Your frustration isn't about miniatures—it's about missing * her*. But " find a different hobby" is a command, not a solution. It's like saying, " * Stop being who you are so I can feel closer to you"* instead of: " * I miss us. Can we try something together? I'd love to see your work and learn from you."* - **Her responsibilities are met (grades, chores), and she's using her own earnings.** $500 from her job is her choice to spend on what she enjoys. * "Would you be this upset if she spent $500 on soccer gear or theater costumes?"* The only difference is your discomfort with the * type* of hobby. - **Hereditary reference is a red herring.** The film's miniatures were a plot device for horror—not a reflection of the hobby itself. Blaming the hobby for your unease projects your own fears onto her. ### **What * would* be " not the asshole" behavior:** - **" I miss our conversations. Can we try a new activity together? I'd love to see your miniatures and learn how you build them."** ( * This shifts focus from " stop doing this" to " let's connect through your interest"*) - **" I'm nervous about her future, but I realize my job is to support her, not dictate her passions. I'll ask her: ' What do you love about miniatures? How can I be part of it?' "** - **" I'm going to therapy to unpack why this hobby triggers me so much. It's not about her—it's about my own anxieties."** ### **The hard truth:** You're not " the asshole" for * caring* about your daughter. But you * are* for **using her hobby as a scapegoat for your own loneliness and unmet needs**. Telling her to " find a different hobby" is controlling, judgmental, and will likely push her further away. **True parenting isn't about reshaping her to fit your vision of " success"— it's about loving her where she is while gently guiding her toward a future * she* chooses.** > 💡 **Try this instead:** > * " I see how much you love this. I'd love to help you build a bigger set sometime. Or maybe we could visit a museum exhibit on miniatures together? I'm curious to learn from you."* > * * (Then actually show up. Listen. Ask questions. Be present.)* > > **This is how you rebuild connection—not by demanding she change, but by choosing to understand her.** > > **Final verdict: 1 ( the asshole)** for the specific action described. > * (But you can absolutely change course. It's not too late to be a better parent to her.)* 💛
